sections.title: 🎯 What You'll Learn
sections.content:
Ever felt like your code is one big, messy blob? Let's fix that! Modularizing code is like organizing your closet - it makes everything easier to find and reuse.

• How to break big problems into small, manageable pieces
• Why methods are your new best friends
• How to write code that's easy to read and maintain

sections.title: 💡 Concept Explanation
sections.content:
Imagine you're building a LEGO castle. Would you try to build it all in one giant piece? No way! You'd build small sections (walls, towers, gates) and then snap them together.

Modularizing code works the same way:

• **Methods** are like LEGO pieces - small, reusable blocks
• Each method does **one specific job** (like calculating tax or printing a receipt)
• You can **reuse** methods anywhere in your program

For example, instead of writing the same code to calculate square roots in 10 places, you write it **once** as a method and call it whenever needed. Cleaner, smarter, and way less typing!

sections.title: ⚡ Key Points
points: ✓ **Single Responsibility**: Each method should do ONE thing well
✓ **Maintainability**: Fix one method, not 100 lines of code
✓ **Testing**: Small methods are easier to test

sections.title: 🔥 Tips & Mistakes
dos: Use methods to avoid code duplication
donts: Don't make methods do multiple unrelated things
sections.protip: If you're copying and pasting code, that's a sign you need a method!

sections.title: 🌍 Real World Use
sections.content: Where is Modularizing Code used in real apps?

examples.how: Separate methods for: calculating discounts, processing payments, generating receipts, and sending confirmation emails
Modular methods for: validating transactions, calculating interest, generating statements, and fraud detection
Methods for: character movement, collision detection, scoring, and rendering graphics

problem.description:
You're building a simple calculator. Right now, all the logic is in one big method. Your task: break it into smaller methods!

Requirements:
• One method for each operation (+, -, *, /)
• One method to get user input
• One method to display results
hints: Start by identifying the different 'jobs' in the code
Each operation (+, -, *, /) should be its own method
The input and output parts can be separate methods too
problem.explanation:
Now each part of the calculator has its own method! This makes the code:
• Easier to read (clear method names)
• Easier to maintain (change one method without breaking others)
• Easier to extend (add new operations without touching existing code)

sections.title: 📝 Summary
points: 📌 Modularizing = breaking code into small, focused methods
📌 Each method should do ONE thing well
📌 Methods make code reusable and easier to maintain
📌 Practice by refactoring big methods into smaller ones
📌 You're now ready to learn about method parameters and return values!
